The Red-bellied grackle Hypopyrrhus pyrohypogaster exhibits a suite of life-history traits characteristic of a slow-paced, long-lived passerine. Field studies conducted in the Colombian Andes indicate that females produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with each clutch containing two to four eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing two to four eggs], a modest fecundity that aligns with the species' extended developmental period. The neonates emerge from calcareous eggs at a remarkably small size, with hatchlings weighing approximately 5.7 grams [Wwb = approximately 5.7 grams], a value that positions them among the lighter altricial newborns relative to adult female mass. The incubation period, measured under controlled conditions at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], lasts approximately 16 days [ab = approximately 16 days], a duration that reflects the energetic demands of embryonic development within a thermally stable environment. This protracted incubation, combined with the modest clutch size, suggests a reproductive strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity.

Laying the groundwork for future reproductive events, the developmental trajectory of juvenile Red-bellied grackles is tightly coupled with the thermal regime typical of their active metabolic periods. Under the species' characteristic active-body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time from hatching to fledging is approximately 17 days [tx = approximately 17 days], a period during which the downy chick undergoes rapid feather development and achieves its first flight. This relatively early fledging age is notable given the bird's altricial start and contrasts with the slower pace of other critical life-history transitions. The achievement of flight represents a key milestone that reduces predation risk and allows the fledgling to access parental food deliveries more effectively, although full nutritional independence is not yet attained at this stage. The species' slow life-history strategy becomes more apparent when considering the extended interval required for the attainment of sexual maturity, which occurs considerably later than fledging. The juvenile bird remains dependent on its natal territory for several weeks post-fledging, gradually refining its foraging skills before dispersing.

Sexual maturation in the Red-bellied grackle is a gradual process that culminates in the attainment of reproductive capacity, though first reproduction is further deferred until a subsequent season. Under the active metabolic conditions maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], male and female juveniles reach the onset of puberty approximately 51 days after hatching [tp = approximately 51 days after hatching], a timing that signals the start of gonadal development rather than immediate breeding capability. This relatively short interval to the initiation of sexual maturation is somewhat deceptive, as the species then enters an extended period of sub-adult life during which individuals refine foraging territories and develop the social skills necessary for successful pair-bonding. The attainment of full adult body mass and the development of the characteristic red belly plumage also occur during this juvenile phase, with females ultimately reaching an asymptotic wet weight of approximately 80 grams [Wwi = approximately 80 grams]. This ultimate body mass represents a near fifteen-fold increase from the hatchling weight, underscoring the substantial somatic investment that precedes reproduction.

A further critical parameter is the age at first reproduction, which field studies have determined to be one year after hatching [tR = one year after hatching], in contrast to the much earlier commencement of gonadal development at approximately 51 days [tp = approximately 51 days] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This prolonged pre-receptive period is typical among tropical passerines where territory acquisition and the development of complex foraging skills delay breeding beyond the point of physiological maturity. Coupled with the maximum reproductive rate of one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year] and the production of two to four eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two to four eggs per clutch], the deferred first breeding imposes a strong constraint on the species' annual fecundity. The single annual reproductive event is thought to be a response to the pronounced seasonality of fruit availability in the montane cloud forest, where the species primarily forages. This combination of delayed first reproduction and low annual output is balanced by the species' high adult survival and multiple potential breeding seasons.

Longevity records for the Red-bellied grackle, compiled from both field observations of color-banded individuals and a small captive colony, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] when individuals are maintained under the typical active-body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a value that places Hypopyrrhus pyrohypogaster among the most long-lived icterids yet recorded, exceeding the eight-year maximum typical of most temperate blackbirds and aligning instead with the extended lifespans observed in Neotropical passerines of the Andean cloud forest. The 80-gram adult body mass in females (80 grams) [Wwi = 80 grams] is associated with a metabolic rate that, although not exceptionally low, is compatible with the extended lifespan typical of tropical forest birds. The combination of a 16-day incubation period (16 days) [ab = 16 days] at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] and a remarkably compressed developmental schedule of approximately 33 days from egg deposition to fledgling independence for this altricial species suggests that the timing of reproduction is constrained primarily by the seasonal availability of arthropod prey rather than by intrinsic physiological limitations.
